observations.text: SP, due to a non-standardized in-flight replanning technique, did not recompute time and fuel to the next turning point before initiating the track modification. The required heading change was applied 14 degrees off the corrected ground track and the aircraft settled 400 feet below the leg altitude. The IP directed the recovery to the planned track and executed part of the fuel recomputation.

SP, due to lack of knowledge of the published procedure for the condition encountered, could not modify the mission profile to avoid the developing cloud layer without assistance, and the RAA for the leg was not stated. The IP directed the track deviation and set the recovery heading, the excursion having reached 25 knots of airspeed and 450 feet of altitude from the planned values before it was contained.

SP modified the flight plan in flight within the desired standards for the Training Section; however, the heading change to regain the planned ground track was applied only after the IP's verbal prompt, and the altitude reached the 300 foot limit before it was corrected. Recognition of the track divergence was delayed on two of the three legs flown. Marginal performance for this stage - timeliness in identifying track and altitude divergence is expected to improve.

SP recognized the deteriorating visibility on the second leg, modified the mission profile in a timely manner and recalculated time and fuel without IP's intervention. Deviations of 180 feet in altitude and 8 degrees in heading during the track correction were self-detected and corrected promptly. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP stated safety altitude per leg and RAA accurately, modified the flight altitude in accordance with the semicircular rule and applied altitude correction technique throughout each turn. Track corrections were computed and flown with precision and speed, holding altitude within 100 feet, airspeed within 6 knots and heading within 4 degrees. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP anticipated the weather build-up before it affected the route, modified the track following the IP's permission and recalculated time and fuel with no prompting. Deviations remained negligible throughout, within 40 feet of altitude, 3 knots of airspeed and 2 degrees of heading, and the aircraft was returned to the planned track by the shortest practicable path. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an unstructured scan between the map, the GPS and the flight instruments, did not identify that the ground track had diverged from the planned leg. The heading correction was never initiated and the aircraft passed 14 degrees off track with airspeed 25 knots below the planned value. The IP directed the turn and roll-out heading and completed the recomputation of time and fuel.

SP, due to failure to shed a secondary task when workload increased, did not modify the flight altitude so that the minimum obstacle altitude for the leg was respected. The aircraft descended 450 feet below the briefed leg altitude before the IP intervened and re-established the safety altitude. Verbal direction was also required for the subsequent track modification.

SP, due to an in-flight fuel calculation performed without reference to time and distance to the next turning point, did not update the flight plan when the leg was extended around the weather. Errors were recognized and corrected only after the IP's verbal prompts, the resulting deviation reaching 300 feet in altitude and 10 degrees in heading at the limit of the standard.

SP, due to continuation of the plan after the information that invalidated it had already been received, did not modify the mission profile when the reported visibility on the third leg fell below the briefed value. The deviation was executed only on the IP's verbal direction, with the aircraft reaching the 20 knot airspeed limit and 300 feet of altitude divergence during the repositioning. Recognition of the developing condition was delayed.

SP planned and executed the in-flight profile modification within the desired standards, applying heading changes to regain the planned ground track without IP's intervention. However, the altitude correction technique during two turns allowed deviations of 250 feet before recovery, and the in-flight fuel figure was accepted only on the second computation. Marginal performance for this stage - consistency in altitude control through correcting turns is expected to improve.

SP identified the unfavorable weather on the outbound leg early, modified the track following the IP's permission and returned to the planned course by the shortest practicable route. Safety altitude per leg and RAA were stated accurately and the recomputed time and fuel were correct, with altitude held within 120 feet, airspeed within 7 knots and heading within 4 degrees. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP conducted a rolling review of the route as the conditions changed, modified the mission profile before the weather became a factor and recalculated time and fuel without error. Altitude, airspeed and heading remained within 50 feet, 3 knots and 2 degrees respectively throughout the replanning and the return to track. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a track modification initiated without first establishing the minimum safe altitude for the new leg, did not respect the obstacle clearance required for the area entered. The IP directed an immediate climb and assumed part of the replanning task, the aircraft having been 500 feet below the applicable safety altitude. Time and fuel figures for the modified route were not produced.

SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the planned track, could not return the aircraft to the route without assistance after the weather deviation. The IP set the recovery heading and executed the recomputation of time and fuel, the aircraft having drifted 16 degrees off the required ground track with 30 knots of airspeed divergence. Further preparation on in-flight replanning is required.

SP, due to an altitude correction technique applied only after the turn was established rather than throughout it, did not hold the modified leg altitude while repositioning around the cloud. The error was recognized and corrected with delay, after the IP's verbal prompt, with the deviation reaching the 300 foot limit. The subsequent heading change to regain track was likewise flown only on verbal direction.

SP, due to mission-completion bias in pressing on past the briefed decision point, did not modify the mission profile when the forecast deterioration materialized on the second leg. The IP's verbal direction was required before the track was changed and time and fuel recalculated, the resulting airspeed divergence reaching the 20 knot limit. The condition had been recognizable well before the correction was applied.

SP, due to a heading correction computed from the GPS track alone without a map cross-reference, over-corrected when returning to the planned ground track. The deviation reached 8 degrees of heading and 220 feet of altitude, recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention. Time and fuel for the modified leg were recomputed correctly.

SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while the in-flight fuel calculation was being completed, did not maintain the modified leg altitude during the correcting turn. Altitude diverged 240 feet and airspeed 16 knots, both detected and corrected promptly without IP's intervention. The remaining legs were flown on the recomputed plan without further error.

SP modified the mission profile and the flight plan in flight within the desired standards, stating safety altitude per leg and RAA correctly and returning to the planned track without IP's intervention. However, the initial heading change on the weather deviation fell 5 degrees short and required a second correction, and the fuel figure was confirmed only on the second computation. Marginal performance for this stage - precision on the first track correction is expected to improve.

SP anticipated the unfavorable conditions, requested the track deviation before the weather became limiting and returned the aircraft to the planned route by the fastest practicable path. Safety altitudes, RAA and the semicircular rule were applied without error, and altitude, airspeed and heading were held within 40 feet, 3 knots and 2 degrees throughout the replanning sequence. Above end of block MIF achieved.
